I created UdaraKita, a web app that monitors and predicts air quality (US AQI) for 12 Indonesian cities. An XGBoost model predicts tomorrow’s AQI from pollutant data (PM2.5, PM10, ozone, NO₂, SO₂, CO), recent AQI history, and seasonal patterns. Results appear with a health category, a prediction range, BMKG and Open-Meteo weather, an interactive map, and three languages (Indonesian, English, Japanese). I built it with FastAPI and React and deployed it on Vercel.

Results: 11 of 12 cities beat the “tomorrow = today” baseline by at least 15%, with an average error reduction of about 29% (best: Makassar, 39%). Jakarta’s error is 8.9 AQI points versus 11.9 for the baseline. The one city that did not pass (Semarang, 11%) does not show a prediction.

One of the fastest ways to trigger a React hydration mismatch in a Next.js App Router application is a single line of date formatting code.

Everything looks completely normal on your local machine. Then you deploy to production, and the browser console throws a hydration error while dates briefly flicker on mobile screens.

Here is why it happens:
Your Next.js Server Component renders the HTML on a Vercel server running in UTC time. When the user opens the page in Jakarta, Sydney, or London, their browser runs client-side hydration using their local timezone and locale settings.

If your component calls new Date().toLocaleDateString() directly during render, the server output and the browser output do not match. React rejects the mismatch and forces an expensive client re-render.

Here are three clean ways we eliminate timezone hydration bugs in production:

1. Lock the Timezone Explicitly on Both Sides:
Never rely on implicit default locales inside Intl.DateTimeFormat or toLocaleDateString. Pass both the locale and an explicit timeZone parameter (for example, 'en-US' and 'UTC' or a stored user timezone preference from the database) so the server and browser produce the exact same string.

2. Defer Local User Timezone Formatting Until Mount:
If you genuinely need the visitor's local browser clock (like "2 hours ago" or local event times), render a deterministic fallback or ISO date on the server, then update to the local string inside a small isolated client wrapper after mount. Never wrap an entire page in a mounted check just to format a timestamp.

3. Pass Serialized ISO Strings Across Server-Client Boundaries:
Pass plain ISO strings from Server Components into Client Components instead of raw Date instances or pre-formatted strings that drop timezone offsets.

Hydration bugs rarely come from complicated business logic. Nine times out of ten, they come from small assumptions about browser globals like window, Date, or invalid nested HTML tags.

Our full range: https://lnkd.in/e338QDVJ

For buyers of palm derivatives, that is a supply-planning signal, not just a headline.

The projection sits alongside the country's B50 biodiesel mandate, which keeps more domestic palm oil at home. Reports also note that this policy shift may raise costs for India's edible oil industry in 2027. Add the EU traceability rules already reshaping export flows, and the direction is clear: less exportable volume, tighter compliance, more competition for certified material.

What this means practically for procurement teams:
1. Contract earlier. Forward coverage on key oleochemical and wax inputs could smooth 2027 exposure.
2. Lock specifications and origin now. Traceability documentation is becoming part of the buying decision, not an afterthought.
3. Diversify supply relationships before the squeeze, not during it.

Nothing here is a price forecast. Export policy, mandate timing and monsoon demand will all shape the outcome, and prices may move either way. But buyers who plan sourcing strategy ahead of a structural export shift tend to have more options than those who react.

A 40-Year-Old Gen Z  😄 

Two years ago, I found myself back in a classroom. Not just any classroom. It's The Apple Developer Academy | Indonesia. What on earth was a 40-year-old career woman doing with coding and design?? 😅

Well, here's the story.

I was the oldest learner in my cohort. Most of my classmates were around 20-ish. Young enough to be my children. 😂 One day, a fellow learner casually told me, “Wow Kak Citra, you're the same age as my mom!”
Well, thank you for the reminder. (And yes, it's Kakak, not Ibu!) 😂

But here's the funny thing: despite the age gap, I never really felt old. For a while, I got to live the Gen Z life. Learning together, laughing at things I didn't always understand, listening to Bernadya's songs, discovering new perspectives, and making friends with some of the most brilliant young minds I've ever met.
It was exhilarating. Almost like..... being young again. 
I even had the incredible opportunity to meet Apple's CEO, Tim Cook. Definitely not something I expected when I decided to go back to school at 40!

But beyond the excitement and unforgettable experiences, the Academy taught me something that challenged the way I had been thinking for years.
I had to learn how to unlearn.
After years of professional experience, I had become pretty good at recognizing patterns, making decisions, and jumping straight into solutions. And that's exactly what I had to unlearn. Here, I discovered that defining the right problem is often more important than finding the right solution.
We spent so much time questioning assumptions, talking to people, challenging our initial interpretations, and resisting the temptation to solve things too quickly. It was uncomfortable at times. Because experience can give you confidence. But it can also make you believe you already know the answer before you've fully understood the question. This experience humbling me to a different level  😅 

And here comes the most unexpected thing I found at the Academy: A part of myself I had almost forgotten.
I actually love being a student! 

After years of working, I was so used to being the person who was expected to know things, have answers, and make decisions. But at the Academy, I could ask the most basic questions, admit I had absolutely NO IDEA what I was doing  🤣, and learn from people half my age.

I didn't realize how much I had missed that feeling until I experienced it again. 🥹 

Thank you, Apple Developer Academy | Indonesia, for the friendships, fresh perspectives, lessons in humility, and for making me feel 20 again. ❤️

Tagging my final project besties: Cyntia Jasmine, Johan Maurits S Sianipar, Arief Yunansyah, Mika Suryofakhri Rahwono, and Muhammad Yusuf 🥰

One vendor quotes you $1,500 a month for an Indonesian developer. Another quotes $2,500. Same country, same role, and both can be honest.

The difference is the level. Our 2026 placement data puts monthly salaries at roughly:
- Junior: $800–1,200
- Mid-level: $1,200–2,000
- Senior: $2,000–3,000
- Staff or principal: $3,000+

To work out which level you need:
1. You can write detailed specs and mentor every day? A junior can work.
2. You already have a senior and need features owned end to end? Mid-level.
3. The work sets technical direction? Senior or above.
4. You're inheriting legacy code? Don't hire junior. Legacy means unknowns.
5. One senior mentoring ten juniors? Keep it to 2–3 per senior.

To check a CV really is mid-level, ask for GitHub history, have the candidate walk through past projects in detail, and run a one-hour technical assessment.

That vetting is what our placement service does. You choose from pre-vetted candidates, and the fee is 2x the hire's monthly salary with a 90-day replacement guarantee. A hire usually takes 2–4 weeks.

The most dangerous device in your office has been printing slides for five years
My feed this morning: "digital apocalypse", Apple, Microsoft, banks and airlines all down at once. 

Before forwarding, I checked.
What actually happened (as of 18 Nov) 
– 13 Nov: Microsoft 365 (Outlook, Teams) down in 70+ countries, into a second day. Microsoft: a technical issue, not cyber. 
– Within days: FAA, United Airlines, Marriott, Charles Schwab, even the NSA's classified internal network. 
– 17 Nov: App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay. Apple blames an internal update; its stores could not ring up sales. 
– US Secretary of State Rubio: "zero evidence" of a malign actor.

So no apocalypse. In a way it is worse: a week of self-inflicted failures showed how few points the world hangs on. A bad update did for free what an attacker would pay for.
Now the part nobody is posting about.

1) Everything above is IT: email, cloud, apps. Painful, but recoverable. OT is the systems that open valves, switch substations and run production lines. There a failure is not an error page. It is darkness, no water, a stopped plant.

2) The way in is rarely the front door. Back in 2019 Microsoft described a state-backed group entering corporate networks through an office printer, a VoIP phone and a video decoder. The printer that has faithfully printed your board decks for five years: default password, no update since installation, on the same flat network as everything else.

3) From the printer to SCADA is a question of segmentation. Dragos found poor IT/OT segmentation in 81% of its 2025 assessments; 73% of its incident cases involved stolen VPN or jump-host credentials. 3,300 industrial companies were hit by ransomware in 2025.

4) It has been done. December 2015, Ukraine: attackers took over SCADA at regional power distributors, and around 225,000 customers lost electricity.

In SEA the cybersecurity conversation still starts and ends with the IT department and a firewall budget. OT sits with engineers who have never met the CISO. Attackers do not respect that org chart.
This week the world went down by accident. 
The question for any CEO running a plant, a grid or a network: who in your company knows exactly what is connected to the production network? 
And when was the printer last updated?

🏙️ How do cities give land back its old jobs: absorbing rain, cooling neighbourhoods and supporting life?

In the November session of the Generation Restoration Dialogues, “Concrete Steps: Restoring Land in and Around Cities”, three speakers who study, plan and design urban land shared what restoration looks like on the ground.

🌱 Sourav Kumar Biswas, director at Sponge Collaborative, a sustainable cities and nature-based solutions specialist, described two 16-acre sites in Chennai. At the first, a degraded water body used as a dumping ground is now a wetland that attracts more than 60 migratory bird species. At the second, a depaved parking lot now holds stormwater from around 100 acres upstream. His message for fast-growing cities: protect what is working first, because “it’s a lot more expensive to undo things and rebuild them the right way than it is to build them right the first time.”
🌱 Anton Siura, Founder and Principal of SIURA Studio, explained how Jakarta’s Tebet Eco Park turned flooding and poor access into an opportunity. The team removed concrete drains, renaturalised the waterway and involved local residents in deciding what the park should offer. He pointed to Singapore’s requirement to replace 100% of the landscape lost to development as a rule that gives everyone “a fair play”.
🌱 Andrea Ramírez-Agudelo, Senior Researcher at United Nations University - Institute for Environment and Human Security (UNU-EHS), reminded us that “cities are uneven by nature”. Degraded, high-risk land is often where the most disadvantaged communities live. Long-term restoration needs everybody at the table from the beginning: communities, designers, engineers, the private sector, researchers and local authorities.

Thank you to our co-host Rossa Mwaniki, Founder of Green Wave Nexus, and to everyone who joined and sent questions.

This week in Jakarta took me back to my roots: Enterprise communication and collaboration technologies. No AI for #TheIntelligentWorkplace this time round.

On behalf of my client, I ran Day 1 of the MuxLab Pre-Sales Certification for channel partners.
 
I’m a commercial person, not an engineer. I learned about the AV and IT technologies over the years. But I believe channel growth doesn’t come from a price list. 

It comes from partners who understand the Brand's value proposition and can design solutions with confidence. So, I built the programme myself: the content, the exercises, the live demos and the certification test.
 
The big discovery of the day: almost nobody in the room had ever had formal AV over IP training. Hence, we started with the basics: 
- The AV over IP triangle: bandwidth, latency and image quality, and how to choose between them.
- Video Codecs, Transmitters, Receivers and Transceivers.
- Control, routing, video wall management and digital signage integration.
 
The key message was simple. UC platforms and endpoints sit on top.

Underneath, someone still has to extend the signal, switch the sources, break out the audio and distribute it all. 

That is where MuxLab fits, over HDMI, HDBaseT or IP. Muximus, the network controller, runs the whole system, routing both video and Dante audio, and it integrates with third-party room control systems.
 
We mixed short presentations, live demos and team design exercises, and finished with a certification test and a lucky draw.
 
For many participants it was their first look at the full MuxLab portfolio. The goal was for every one of them to leave able to design on MuxLab, and the energy in the room told me we were on the right track.

Two weeks in Southeast Asia. A clearer view of what’s next for SANS SOUCI.

Singapore → Kuala Lumpur → Jakarta → back to Singapore.

Over the past two weeks, I met with local partners, interior designers, developers, architects and our Asia team. As Chief Sales Officer, I value time on the ground. It helps me make better decisions about where to invest, which partnerships to deepen and how best to support our team in the region.

The trip reinforced something I’ve long believed. In a global business, relationships grow through collaboration across markets. A conversation in Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta or Bangkok can lead to a project anywhere in the world.

Our next steps will soon take shape, starting with a new SANS SOUCI showroom in Singapore. We’re creating an experience centre where designers and local partners can see our lighting firsthand and collaborate with our team.

Thank you to everyone who made time to meet with me, and to our Asia team for building these relationships every day.
